Required rather than optional: a contract without a version cannot

ContractEdges.description:
The contract edges a C4 element owns: the interfaces it publishes, and
the interfaces it depends on.

Declared once and inherited by all four blueprint types rather than
repeated on each, because the same fact recorded at four altitudes
under three different spellings is how a vocabulary drifts. An element
provides a contract at whichever altitude it happens to sit; the
property is named for the concept, not for the level.

These are not the neighbour edges ADR-009 reserves to a parent. A
neighbour relationship varies by host — a shared module has different
collaborators in every container that composes it, which is why no
single outward list is correct and the parent owns it. A contract is a
named document with one identity, and the fact that an element
publishes or depends on it holds wherever that element is composed. So
this edge belongs to the element, and ADR-009's rule is untouched.

URL are exempt. Defaults to the active profile's registered value.

DocumentFrontmatter.description:

Membership in the corpus is determined by this envelope rather than by

`type` is a specification, wherever it sits in the tree. Each document
type extends this struct with its own relationship and classification
properties, so the envelope is validated identically everywhere and only
the extension differs.

DocumentType.description:
The classification of a specification document.

A document's type selects the schema, slug pattern and required sections
that govern it. This is the controlled vocabulary the spec-driven-dev
profile registers; a repository whose documents declare a type outside
this set is recorded as excluded with reason `unknown-type` rather than
being checked against the wrong rules.

DocumentTypeRegistration.description: Everything the engine needs to check one document type.

numbered.description:
Whether documents of this type carry a sequence number the CLI can
derive the next value of.

Numbering is global per type: the next number is one greater than the
highest in use anywhere in the corpus, regardless of directory.

pairings.description: Relationship properties that must be declared from both ends.

reference_properties.description:
Frontmatter properties of this type that hold document references.

A value in one of these properties that matches no corpus member's
slug is reported the same way an unresolved `[[slug]]` in the body is.

schema.description:
The JSON Schema this type's frontmatter is validated against,
expressed as a JSON Pointer into the bundled schema or as a path to a
standalone one.

section_sets.description:
Named sets of headings a span query can select, so a reviewing agent
can ask for the normative sections of a document and read only those.

sections.description: The heading hierarchy a document of this type must contain.

slug_pattern.description:
The pattern a document of this type must match in its `slug`.

A mismatch is reported with both the actual slug and this pattern
quoted, so the finding is self-contained and the fixing agent needs no
further lookup.

ElementRecord.description:
The three fields that identify any element the framework names.

This is the smallest unit of description in the vocabulary, and it is
deliberately shared by two artifacts that look unrelated. A child element
a parent document declares inline — a component of a container, a module
of a system — carries exactly these fields in a fenced record block. A
child that has been promoted to its own document carries them as the
opening of its frontmatter, because `DocumentFrontmatter` inherits them.

One schema therefore validates a child in either state, which is what
makes promotion a lift-and-link operation rather than a re-authoring
one: the record block moves verbatim into the new document's
frontmatter, and every parent roster replaces the block with a link.

the reader.

FeatureBlueprint.description:
A transient change document describing how the system changes to deliver
one feature.

Unlike the blueprints it modifies, a feature blueprint describes a
change rather than a state, so it reaches `in-progress` and then
`retired` rather than `active`. Its `updates` and `creates` properties
are what let tooling derive when the change is complete: the feature is
not done until every document it names has been updated or activated.

created_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of the document's creation. Optional.

creates.description:
Slugs of new documents authored alongside this blueprint, such as
draft contracts for interfaces the feature introduces.

delivery.description:
The delivery unit grooming plans against. When `staged`, each stage
boundary is enumerated in the blueprint's Sequencing Constraints.

description.description:

plan.description:

task files. Absent before grooming, since an ungroomed blueprint has
no plan yet; present through `retired`, since the pointer retires
with the document rather than being cleared.

Finding.description:
One reported conformance result.

Every check in this tool reports through this shape, so a consumer
renders one thing and a check added later is readable by a consumer
written before it. The five common properties are what make a diagnostic
self-contained — the rule that raised it, how badly it bears on the run,
which file, where in that file, and what is wrong — and `detail` carries
the same information again in structured form for a consumer that acts
on it rather than printing it.

detail.description: The structured form of the same defect.

message.description:
What is wrong, stating the violated constraint and the value that
violated it, so the finding needs no further lookup to act on.

path.description:
The file the finding is against, relative to the repository root and
written with forward slashes on every platform.

position.description:
Where in the file the finding is, as a span rather than a bare line
number, so a report can point at a value inside a line.

rule.description: The check that raised this finding.

severity.description: How badly this finding bears on the run.

FindingDetail.description:
The structured detail of one finding, selected by the kind of defect.

Every finding carries one. The message on the finding is derivable from
this value, so a consumer branches on structure rather than parsing
prose, and a renderer that wants to offer a fix reads the fields it needs
as values.

The union is open to extension in the sense that matters: a later check
adds a variant without changing the envelope that carries it, and a
consumer that does not recognise a variant still has the rule
identifier, the severity, the path, the span and the message.

FindingDuplicateSlug.description:
A slug declared by more than one corpus member.

Reported against each of the two documents, each naming the other, so
that checking either one surfaces the collision.

other_path.description:
The other document's path, relative to the repository root and written
with forward slashes on every platform.

FindingMissingProperty.description:
A property the document's type requires and the document does not
declare.

Modelled apart from the general schema violation because a missing
property is the most common defect by a wide margin, and a consumer
offering to insert one needs the property name as a value rather than as
a substring of a message.

pointer.description: The JSON Pointer of the object that should carry the property.

property.description: The name of the property that is absent.

FindingReport.description:
Everything one check run produced.

The two collections answer different questions and neither substitutes
for the other. `findings` is what is wrong; `checks` is what was looked
at. A report carrying no findings is only good news if every check the
caller cares about is accounted for in `checks` as having passed.

Both are lists rather than maps so that the emitter owns their order and
can make output byte-identical across platforms without a change to this
model.

checks.description:
Every check the run knows about, in the order the emitter fixes, each
with what became of it.

findings.description: Every finding the run produced, in the order the emitter fixes.

FindingSchemaViolation.description:
A frontmatter value that violates the schema its document type is
validated against.

The pointer and the constraint together make the finding actionable
without re-running the validator: the pointer says which property, and
the constraint says what it had to satisfy.

constraint.description: The constraint the value failed, quoted as the schema states it.

pointer.description:
The JSON Pointer at which the violation occurred, relative to the
document's frontmatter.

value.description:
The offending value, as raw source text rather than as a YAML parser
reinterpreted it, so a date written unquoted is reported as it was
written.

FindingSlugPattern.description:
A slug that does not match the pattern the active profile supplies for
the document's type.

Both halves are carried so the finding is self-contained: an agent
fixing it needs neither the profile nor the document open.

pattern.description: The pattern the active profile supplies for this document's type.

FindingUnverified.description:
A check that was requested and could not run.

This is the structured half of the `unverified` severity: the reason
states what was missing, so a consumer can decide whether to install a
dependency, adjust configuration, or accept the gap.

reason.description:
Why the check could not run, stated so that it needs no further lookup
to act on.

IndexEntry.description:
One corpus member in the index: where it lives and what its frontmatter
declares.

The entry is deliberately additive. This sprint populates the path and
the frontmatter envelope; later features attach headings, extracted
record blocks and references to the same entry under the same
`schema_version`, and no property here forecloses modelling references
as their own collection later.

frontmatter.description:
The member's parsed frontmatter.

Absent exactly when `parse_error` is present: a document whose
frontmatter could not be parsed is still indexed, but it has no parsed
envelope to carry.

parse_error.description:
The failure that prevented this member's frontmatter from being
parsed, with its position.

Present exactly when `frontmatter` is absent. A member carrying this
property does not make the index a failure; the index is still emitted
and still contains every other document.

path.description:
The member's path, relative to the repository root and written with
forward slashes on every platform.

IndexExclusion.description: One candidate file that is not a corpus member, and why.

path.description:
The excluded file's path, relative to the repository root and written
with forward slashes on every platform.

reason.description: Why the file is not a member.

type.description:
The `type` value the file declared, reported when `reason` is
`unknown-type` so that a reviewing agent can judge whether the profile
or the document is wrong.

components.description:

children have been promoted to documents of their own.

A child is in exactly one state: promoted and linked here, or

The module's semantic version.

ParseError.description:
A located failure to parse part of a document.

Recorded against the document it occurred in rather than raised, because
one unparsable file must not cost a repository the index of every other
file. The position is a `Span`, like every other position this framework
reports.

message.description:
What could not be parsed, stated so that the message needs no further
lookup to act on.

position.description: Where in the document the failure occurred.

name.description:
The name of a registered profile.

Exactly one profile applies per invocation. A value naming no
registered profile is reported as a finding listing the names that are
registered, rather than as a bare startup failure.

ProfileRegistration.description:
What a profile registers into Document Core.

**Internal surface.** This is the vocabulary a profile hands to the
engine in-process, not something an adopting repository authors. It is
not reachable from `specs.toml` in v1 and is not an extension point
outside this repository; `[profile].name` selects one of these
registrations by name, and that naming is the whole of the relationship
between the two halves of the configuration contract.

It is modelled here rather than left to hand-written Go for two
reasons. Registration is data — type names, patterns, section trees,
block tags — and only the rules that cannot be expressed as data stay in
code. And the open question of which internal keys get promoted to the
public surface is answered by editing this struct, which is a smaller
and more reviewable act than editing an interface and its
implementations.

Property names are snake_case throughout, matching the public surface,
so that promoting a key to `specs.toml` is a move rather than a rename.

block_tags.description:
Fenced block info strings whose contents are parsed as structured data
and attached to the containing document and heading.

conventions.description:
The convention values this profile supplies when `specs.toml` omits
them.

document_types.description:
The document types this profile defines, keyed by the value documents
declare in their `type` property.

A markdown file declaring a type absent from this map is recorded as
excluded with reason `unknown-type` and its declared value reported,
so a reviewing agent can judge whether the profile or the document is
wrong.

finished_statuses.description:
The statuses at which a document is considered finished, and therefore
at which leftover template placeholders are a defect rather than
work in progress.

name.description: The name an adopting repository writes in `[profile].name`.

placeholder_patterns.description:
Patterns whose presence in a finished document indicates unreplaced
template scaffolding.

PropertyPairing.description:
One half of a relationship that must be declared from both ends.

A blueprint naming a child in `children` where that child declares no
`parent_slug` is a half-built edge, and it is reported against both
documents rather than only the one that happens to be checked first.

counterpart.description: The property the referenced document must declare in return.

property.description: The property declared on this document.

Rfc.description:
An improvement proposal raised against a skill by a run that exercised
it.

The provenance properties below are the load-bearing part. A skill
behaves differently under different models, efforts and harnesses, so a
defect real under one may not reproduce under another, and triage cannot
scope a fix without knowing which run saw it. They are recorded
faithfully by the retro that raises the RFC and judged by the triage
that receives it — the two roles are deliberately separate.

created_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of the document's creation. Optional.

description.description:
A one- to two-sentence summary of what this element is and what it is
responsible for.

On C4 blueprints this is the brief description rendered on diagrams,
so it is written to be read at a glance rather than as an
introduction.

effort.description:
The reasoning effort the run used.

Left unconstrained because the effort vocabulary belongs to the
harness rather than to this framework, and `unknown` is a legitimate
value when a transcript does not record it.

model.description:
The exact model identifier the run used — not a family name. A finding
that reproduces under one model and not another is scoped by this
property alone.

origin.description:
Where the run happened: `self` when this repository critiqued its own
skill, otherwise the name of the project the run took place in.

plugin_version.description: The plugin version the critiqued skill shipped in.

related.description:
Peer documents relevant to this one without a stronger relationship:
the ADRs behind it, the standards it observes.

Every relationship property in this vocabulary names documents by
slug, and every named slug must resolve to a corpus member.

runs_observed.description:
How many runs stand behind the evidence.

This is the denominator for any claim about recurrence: an RFC may not
assert more recurrence than it observed.

severity.description: The highest severity among this RFC's proposals.

skill_version.description:
The version recorded in the critiqued skill's own frontmatter at the
time of the run, so triage can tell whether a defect has already been
fixed since.

RfcSeverity.description:
How badly a run was impeded by the skill an RFC critiques.

An RFC carries the highest severity among its proposals, so that triage
can rank a queue without opening every document.

RuleId.description:
The identifier of one check, stable across releases.

Every finding names the rule that raised it, and the run report accounts
for every rule it knows about, so the identifier is the join between the
two: a caller naming a subset of checks to run names them by these
values, and reads the outcome of each back under the same value.

Identifiers are namespaced kebab-case — `slug/pattern-mismatch`,
`frontmatter/missing-property` — so the family a check belongs to is
legible without a lookup table. The shape is stated rather than
constrained because a Strata regex literal cannot contain a forward
slash.

Section.description:
A required heading, and the headings required beneath it.

Required sections are a hierarchy rather than a flat list because the
defects worth catching are about nesting: a missing `## Consequences`
and a `### Consequences` misfiled under `## Decision` are different
problems, and a flat list cannot tell them apart.

children.description: Headings required one level beneath this one.

repeated.description:
Whether the heading occurs once per instance of something in the
document rather than exactly once — one subsection per alternative
considered, for example.

Without this distinction a section tree can only describe documents of
fixed shape, and not all of the templates this framework ships are
fixed.

required.description: Whether a document of this type must contain the heading.

Severity.description:
How badly a finding bears on a run.

The three values are the whole vocabulary, and the distinction that
matters most is the third: `unverified` is not a milder failure, it is
the absence of a result. A check the tool was asked to perform and could
not run reports `unverified` rather than passing silently, because a
consumer that cannot tell the two apart will read a missing check as a
clean one.

Slug.description:
A cross-reference identifier for a specification document.

Every relationship between documents is expressed as a slug rather than a
path, so moving a file never breaks a reference. Slugs are kebab-case:
lowercase alphanumeric words joined by single hyphens.

Span.description:
A contiguous region of a document.

Byte offset and byte length are the authoritative extent, because spans
address regions *within* a line as well as whole sections — a malformed
`slug` value occupies part of a line, not the line itself. Line and
column are carried alongside for readability: they are what a human or
an agent reads in a report, and they are derived from the offset rather
than being an independent source of truth.

Lines and columns are one-based. A column counts Unicode codepoints from
the start of its line, matching the way this framework's conventions
measure width, so an em dash advances the column by one rather than by
its three UTF-8 bytes.

end_column.description: One-based codepoint column one past the last codepoint of the region.

end_line.description: One-based line on which the region ends.

length.description:
Length of the region in bytes. Zero is a valid, empty region — the
content of `---\n---` is an empty span rather than an absent one.

offset.description:
Byte offset of the first byte of the region, from the start of the
document.

start_column.description: One-based codepoint column at which the region starts.

start_line.description: One-based line on which the region starts.

SpecIndex.description:
The machine-readable description of a repository's specification corpus,
emitted to the file **specs.json** in the configured spec root.

This is the artifact CI, agents and a central architecture catalogue all
read instead of each re-deriving the corpus. It crosses a boundary, so
its shape is defined once here and generated into JSON Schema, Go and
Markdown rather than being assembled by hand in the emitter.

The model is additive by design: later features add properties to it and
to its entries under the same `schema_version`. `entries` and
`exclusions` are lists rather than maps precisely so that the emitter
owns their order and can make output byte-identical across platforms
without a change to this model.

entries.description: Every corpus member, in the order the emitter fixes.

exclusions.description: Every excluded candidate file, in the order the emitter fixes.

input_hash.description:
A hash of everything this index was built from, written as
`sha256:` followed by lowercase hexadecimal.

This is what makes the emitted file double as a warm cache: a later
invocation recomputes the hash of the corpus's current inputs and
serves this index unchanged when the two agree, rather than
rebuilding. It is a hash of **content** — every candidate file's
repository-relative path and bytes, plus the active profile's
vocabulary — and never of modification time, so a fresh checkout
whose files all carry new timestamps and identical content is still
served warm.

Absent on an index that was not built by walking a corpus. An index
carrying no hash is never served warm; it is rebuilt.

schema_version.description:
The version of this index's schema.

Pinned to `1.0` for as long as the shape only grows. A change to the
shape of what is already here — as opposed to an addition alongside it
— updates this value and the emitted index in the same change.

workspace.description:
The workspace identifier from configuration, so that indexes emitted
by several repositories can be merged into one graph without two
documents that both declare `adr-001` colliding.

SpecsConfig.description:
The `specs.toml` file an adopting repository authors at its root.

This is the public half of the configuration contract: the surface teams
outside the CLI's own team write, and therefore the surface whose
compatibility promise costs something to keep. It is deliberately small.
A repository says which repository it is, where its documents live,
which profile is active, and a short list of house conventions —
and nothing else.

In particular there is no way to define a document type, register a
block tag, or supply a schema from here. Those belong to the profile,
and holding them back is what keeps the promise cheap: a key that was
never public cannot be broken by changing it. Promotion runs one way and
is additive, so a repository that never wrote a key it could not write
is unaffected by a later version that lets it.

Undeclared keys are a defect rather than a courtesy. A misspelled key is
far more common than a key from the future, and silently ignoring one
would let a repository believe it had configured something it had not.

conventions.description:
House conventions. Every key resolves from the active profile when
absent, so the whole table may be omitted.
